about: Prerequisite map for P4 Atomic structure (brief docs/briefs/2026-11-27-phase-c-physics.md, Phase C B1, 2026-11-27): every idea the four scripted lessons use, what each depends on (maths included), and where it is taught. Lessons run in syllabus order: p4-nuclear-model, p4-radioactivity, p4-half-life, p4-nuclear-fission. P1 to P3 come first, so energy, kinetic energy, mass, density and particles may be recalled. Used when scripting: each script teaches or recalls an idea before it asks about it.

ideas.name: Everything is made of atoms; an element has one kind of atom
ideas.taught: KS3 science; p3-particle-model key point 1; p4-nuclear-model basics

ideas.name: Positive and negative charge; opposites attract, like charges repel
Mass; dense = a lot of mass in a small space
A scientific model explains what cannot be seen; it changes when new evidence does not fit
ideas.taught: p3-particle-model key point 4; p4-nuclear-model basics and key point 1

ideas.name: Standard form: 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 0.0000000001 m
Tiny indivisible spheres, then the electron (Thomson) and the plum pudding model: positive charge spread out, electrons embedded

Alpha particles (positive) fired at thin gold foil: most straight through (empty space), a few deflected a lot (charge concentrated), very few back (tiny dense positive nucleus with most of the mass); nuclear model replaces plum pudding
Atom radius about 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; nucleus radius under 1/10 000 of it; protons (+1, mass 1), neutrons (0, mass 1) in the nucleus, electrons (−1, very small) outside
Atomic number = protons (decides the element); mass number = protons + neutrons; neutrons = mass number − atomic number; symbol notation, mass number on top
ideas.taught: p4-nuclear-model key point 3; recalled in p4-radioactivity

ideas.name: Isotopes: same protons, different neutrons; an atom has no overall charge; an ion has lost or gained electrons
Bohr: electrons at specific distances (energy levels); absorb electromagnetic radiation = move up, further out; emit = move down, closer in; protons, then neutrons (Chadwick) found later
Unstable nuclei decay at random, giving out radiation; activity in becquerels (Bq); count rate from a Geiger-Muller tube
Ionising: radiation knocks electrons off atoms, making ions
Alpha: 2 protons + 2 neutrons (a helium nucleus); stopped by paper or a few cm of air; most ionising; mass number −4, atomic number −2
Beta: a fast electron from the nucleus (a neutron turns into a proton); stopped by a few mm of aluminium; moderately ionising; mass number same, atomic number +1
Gamma: electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus; only reduced by thick lead or concrete; least ionising; no change to either number
Background radiation: natural (radon from rocks, cosmic rays) and man-made (medical X-rays, fallout, accidents); dose in sieverts depends on place and job
Nuclear equations: mass numbers and atomic numbers balance on each side
Halving; (½)ⁿ; fractions 1/2, 1/4, 1/8
Half-life: time for the number of unstable nuclei, or the activity, to halve; random decay but predictable in large numbers; A₀ × (½)ⁿ; net decline as a ratio
Decay graph: activity against time, a curve that never reaches zero; half-life read between any value and half of it
Tracers (gamma, short half-life) and radiotherapy (gamma beam or a source inside, near a tumour); benefit against risk; perceived risk
Irradiation (exposed; does not become radioactive) versus contamination (radioactive atoms on or in it); dangers (DNA damage, mutations, cancer); half-life and hazard; protection; peer review
Kinetic energy: energy of a moving object

Fission: a large unstable nucleus (U-235, Pu-239) absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei of similar size, giving out 2 or 3 neutrons, gamma rays and energy; all products have kinetic energy
Chain reaction: the neutrons cause more fissions; uncontrolled = a nuclear weapon; controlled in a reactor (some neutrons absorbed, one more fission each on average)
Fusion: two light nuclei join into a heavier one; some mass becomes the energy of radiation; powers stars; not yet a large-scale power source
